evidence.quote: This specification contains no technical changes from the Experimental RFC 7238, which it obsoletes.

finalText:
## 301 vs. 308

**What each means.** Both codes say a resource has moved to a new URL for good. RFC 9110 uses the same wording for both. For 301 it says "the target resource has been assigned a new permanent URI and any future references to this resource ought to use one of the enclosed URIs", and the 308 section repeats it word for word (https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc9110.html). In both cases the server SHOULD send a `Location` header with the new URL, and the client MAY follow it automatically. The only real difference is what happens to the request method and body.

**Request method and body.**
- **301:** For historical reasons, a client MAY turn a POST into a GET when it follows a 301 (https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc9110.html).
  - **History:** RFC 9110 explains that early browsers disagreed on this, most ended up switching to GET, and 301 was later changed to allow it.
  - **What gets resent:** RFC 9110's general redirect rules say the client should resend the original request with a few listed changes. One change is adjusting the method if the status code allows it. If the method becomes GET or HEAD, the client removes content headers such as Content-Type and Content-Length, so the body is dropped too.
  - **Browsers:** MDN says the WHATWG Fetch Standard, which browsers follow, handles a 301 in response to a POST by sending a GET (https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/HTTP/Reference/Status/301).
- **308:** 308 exists to be the permanent redirect that keeps the method.
  - **RFC 7538:** It calls 308 "similar to 301 (Moved Permanently) … except that it does not allow changing the request method from POST to GET" (https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc7538.html).
  - **What gets resent:** Since the method can't change, the client resends the original request, body included, to the new URL. MDN says the method and body are not modified, and that changing the method after a 308 is prohibited (https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/HTTP/Reference/Status/308, https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/HTTP/Reference/Status/301).
  - **Where the rule comes from:** RFC 9110's 308 section doesn't state this rule itself. Its 307 section does say the method MUST NOT change. For 308, the rule comes from the general redirect rules and the history note, which says 307 and 308 were added to mark redirects that keep the method.

**Where sources disagree.** MDN's 308 page says a 301 "requires the request method and the body to remain unchanged", and that older clients get this wrong by switching to GET. That conflicts with RFC 9110, which explicitly lets clients switch POST to GET on a 301. It also conflicts with MDN's own 301 page, which says the switch is "permitted by the HTTP specification". RFC 9110 is the authoritative text, so the 308 page's statement looks outdated. I couldn't open the Fetch Standard itself (fetch.spec.whatwg.org returned 404), so the browser behaviour above relies on MDN's summary.

**Caching.** RFC 9110 calls both 301 and 308 "heuristically cacheable". That means a cache may store them and estimate how long they stay fresh, unless the request method or explicit cache controls say otherwise. RFC 9111 (HTTP Caching) adds that a cache may estimate freshness only when no explicit expiry time is given. It also notes that older specs called this "cacheable by default", which is the term RFC 7538 used for 308 (https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc9111.html, https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc7538.html). In practice, a cached 301 or 308 can keep sending clients to the new URL unless the server sets explicit cache headers.

**Where they are specified now.** Both are defined in RFC 9110, HTTP Semantics (June 2022): 301 in Section 15.4.2 and 308 in Section 15.4.9.
- RFC 9110 obsoletes RFC 7231, the old home of 301, and RFC 7538, the standalone 308 spec.
- RFC 7538 had itself replaced the experimental RFC 7238, with no technical changes (https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc9110.html, https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc7538.html).
- RFC 9110 notes that 308 dates from June 2014, much later than the other redirect codes, so some clients may not recognize it.
- RFC 7538 says to use 308 only when the server is confident the client understands it, or when falling back to 300 (Multiple Choices) behaviour would not cause problems.

**In short:** use 301 for permanent moves where the client only fetches the page with GET. Use 308 for permanent moves where a POST or PUT and its body must reach the new URL unchanged.
